The Work, Teaching and Leadership of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: Reshaping Judaism in an Age of Crisis and Reconstruction
This source surveys the figure of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, the leader who reshaped Judaism after the destruction of the Second Temple. The text details how Ribaz acted with political shrewdness toward the Roman Empire in order to save the world of Torah, and how he established the spiritual center at Yavneh as a substitute for political sovereignty in Jerusalem. Through a series of halakhic enactments and theological reforms, he moved the focus of atonement and holiness from the sacrificial service to acts of loving-kindness and the study of Torah, thereby securing the nation's survival in exile. Beyond his public work, the source discusses him as a humble educator who stressed the importance of a good heart and of shared study, presenting his relations with his five outstanding disciples and his formative influence on later generations.
The Work, Teaching and Leadership of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: Reshaping Judaism in an Age of Crisis and Reconstruction
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's Standing in the Schools of Hillel and Shammai, and His Conception of Torah Study
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai (called Zakkai or Zakkayi in the literature of the Land of Israel, and "Ribaz" for short) was active in the first century CE and became the key figure in the dramatic transition of the Jewish people from the destruction of the Second Temple to an era of reconstruction and halakhic creativity.[1, 2, 3] Ribaz acquired his Torah from Hillel the Elder and Shammai the Elder.[1, 2, 3, 4] In the school of Hillel's disciples, which numbered eighty outstanding students, Ribaz was classed as "the least of them all," while Jonathan ben Uzziel was classed as "the greatest of them all."[5] This classification of Hillel's disciples placed thirty of them as worthy of having the Divine Presence rest upon them as it did upon Moses our teacher, thirty as worthy of intercalating the year, and twenty as middling.[5]
Despite his classification as "least" in the school—a designation that points to his being the youngest of the disciples or the last of them—Ribaz displayed complete mastery of every recess of the Oral Torah.[5] It was said of him that he left unstudied no Scripture, Mishnah, Gemara, halakhot, aggadot, Tosefta, fine points of the Torah or fine points of the scribes, light matters and weighty ones, verbal analogies (gezerot shavot), calendrical cycles, gematriot, and even esoteric fields such as the speech of the ministering angels, the speech of demons, the speech of palm trees, and the parables of launderers and foxes.[3, 5, 6] This recognition of his abilities led Hillel the Elder to grant him the formative title "father of wisdom and father of the generations," defining him as a head of the sages and a guide for all the generations to come.[3, 6, 7]
Ribaz's educational teaching completely rejected intellectual and scholarly arrogance.[7] Although he had acquired phenomenal knowledge, he used to warn his many disciples against conceit, saying: "If you have learned much Torah, do not take credit for yourself—for it was for this that you were created."[4, 5, 8] This remark reflects a profound cosmic conception, according to which Torah is not an act of personal heroism that confers privilege or honor, but a fundamental existential duty.[4, 5] Human existence is conditional upon accepting the Torah and laboring in it, as emerges from the tradition that the Holy One, blessed be He, stipulated with the work of Creation that if Israel does not accept the Torah, the world will revert to chaos and void; study is therefore the fulfillment of a condition of Creation and not a voluntary act of piety.[4]
Ribaz's way of life exemplified a complete synthesis between rigorous scholarship and humility and social piety.[7] He took care to be the first to arrive at the study hall, did not waste a moment of his learning, and never engaged in idle talk or walked four cubits without Torah and tefillin.[3, 6, 7] His moral path stressed love of fellow creatures and being first to greet every person in the marketplace, even gentiles.[6, 7]
In the economic and social sphere, Ribaz developed a distinctive doctrine concerning the commandment of charity.[7] He demanded that those around him give charity abundantly and used to say that he gives nothing of his own but only from the Creator's property, so there is no reason to be tight-fisted.[7] In his view, although a person's sustenance is apportioned to him from one Rosh Hashanah to the next, God deducts the charity money a person has given from the list of losses and afflictions decreed against him, so that charity becomes an economic and spiritual shield.[7]
This conception of the protection afforded by Torah and charity found expression when a Jerusalem family came to him, all of whose sons had died before the age of eighteen.[7, 9] Ribaz identified them as descendants of Eli the priest, upon whom early death had been decreed because of the sins of Hophni and Phinehas, and proposed that they engage in Torah and acts of loving-kindness as a spiritual protective mechanism that would free them from the curse.[7, 9] The members of the family accepted his advice, engaged in Torah and kindness, and lived long lives.[7, 9]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Political Policy and the Edicts Against Zealotry on the Eve of the Destruction
During the Great Revolt and the Roman siege of Jerusalem, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai stood out as a moderate, peace-seeking leader who preferred political compromise to hopeless military zealotry.[3] Like his teacher Hillel, Ribaz recoiled from acts of religious zealotry that take no account of political reality.[3] His pragmatic position was formulated in his well-known warning against demolishing the high places and foreign cults of the gentiles in the Land of Israel: "Do not rush to tear down the gentiles' high places lest you be made to build them with your own hands—lest you tear down ones of brick and they tell you, 'Make them of stone'; of stone, and they tell you, 'Make them of wood.'"[3] This warning reflects a strategic view that understands that zealous acts of provocation against foreign authorities do not help to purify the land but invite a harsh counter-reaction and worsen the burden of subjugation and the destruction of the Jewish settlement.[3]
When the siege of Jerusalem began, Ribaz sat inside the city and watched with alarm the conduct of the zealot factions, called in the sources "the biryonim" (the thugs).[3] The zealots burned the city's stores of grain and food in order to force the inhabitants to fight the Romans out of despair.[3] Ribaz, who saw people boiling straw in order to drink its water because of deep hunger, understood that the city could not withstand the siege of the commander Vespasian and that continued fighting would lead to mass slaughter and the extinction of Torah.[3] He concluded that the zealots' plans must be foiled and that he must flee the city in order to save the core of the spiritual leadership.[1, 3]
The plan to smuggle him out of Jerusalem was based on deceiving the zealot guards at the city gates.[1, 3] Ribaz turned in secret to the head of the biryonim, Abba Sikra (ben Batiah), who was his nephew, and enlisted his help.[3] Following his instruction, Ribaz feigned serious illness and then death.[3] His two outstanding disciples, Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananiah, placed him in a coffin and carried him to the city gates, knowing that the zealots permitted the dead to be taken out for burial outside the walls because of the sanctity of Jerusalem.[3, 10]
At the city gates the operation faced a real danger of failure.[3] The zealot guards suspected the coffin and wished to stab it with a sword or push it to make sure of death.[3] Abba Sikra prevented them with tactical arguments, warning that such acts would disgrace the leader's honor in the eyes of the public ("They will say: they stabbed the Rabban, they pushed the Rabban").[3] The guards withdrew, and Ribaz was successfully smuggled outside the walls directly to the Roman camp.[3, 10]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Meeting with Vespasian: The Paradox of the Honey Barrel and the Dragon, and the Strategy of "Hatzalah Portah"
Upon reaching the Roman camp, Ribaz met the commander Vespasian and addressed him with the royal greeting "Peace upon you, O king."[3, 10] Vespasian reacted in anger and claimed that Ribaz was a rebel liable to death twice: first, because he called him king though he was not king; and second, because if he really was king, why had Ribaz not come to him until now.[3, 8, 10, 11] Ribaz answered his questions with political and exegetical shrewdness.[12] To the first question he replied that Vespasian was soon to be appointed emperor, since the Temple and Jerusalem are destined to fall only into the hands of a king, as it is said, "And Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one," and "mighty" means nothing other than a king.[12] To the second question he replied that the biryonim who ruled Jerusalem had prevented him from leaving and coming to him.[12]
While they were conversing, an official Roman messenger arrived and informed Vespasian that the emperor had died and that the notables of Rome had appointed him the new emperor.[3, 10, 12] The event brought a dramatic turn in the emperor's attitude toward Ribaz.[3, 10] Vespasian valued the Tanna's wisdom and offered him to ask one request that he would fulfill for him.[3, 10]
In the course of this discussion, Vespasian presented Ribaz with a pointed parable challenging his moderate path [12]: "If people had a barrel of honey with a dragon (serpent) coiled around it, would they not break the barrel in order to kill the dragon?" In this parable the barrel represents Jerusalem and the Temple, and the dragon represents the rebel zealots. Vespasian argued that there was no escaping the destruction of the entire city in order to eradicate the rebels within it.[12] Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was silent and did not answer this parable.[12]
Ribaz's silence drew pointed criticism from later sages.[8, 10, 11] The Gemara notes that Rav Yosef (some say Rabbi Akiva) applied to him the verse "He turns wise men backward, and makes their knowledge foolish," claiming that he should have answered Vespasian: "We take tongs, we remove the dragon and kill it, and we leave the barrel alone" (that is, one takes tongs, removes the serpent and kills it, and leaves the barrel whole).[12] According to this criticism, Ribaz missed a historic opportunity to demand the rescue of Jerusalem and the Temple from the Romans.[8, 10, 11]
But Ribaz's silence and his limited requests stemmed from a calculated strategy of political realism.[8, 10, 11] Ribaz assessed that too large a demand for the rescue of all of Jerusalem would be rejected out of hand by an emperor determined to display a crushing military victory, and as a result everything would be lost.[8, 10, 11] He chose to prefer the strategy of "hatzalah portah" (a small but certain rescue) in order to secure the nation's future, and made three focused requests [8, 10, 11]:
"Give me Yavneh and its sages": saving the sages of the generation and establishing a Torah and legal center as an alternative to Jerusalem.[3, 10, 13]
"The dynasty (shushilta) of Rabban Gamliel": ensuring the safety of the members of the patriarchal family of the House of Hillel, in order to preserve legitimate and recognized national leadership and to prevent anarchy.[3, 10]
"And physicians to heal Rabbi Zadok": doctors who would heal Rabbi Zadok, who was a symbol of the righteous man who had fasted forty consecutive years to prevent the destruction and whose body was in extreme mortal danger.[3, 10]
Through these three requests, Ribaz laid the foundation for the continued existence of the people of Israel as a living, developing spiritual community without need of a sovereign political and Temple center.[1, 3, 13]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Enactments at Yavneh as the Foundation for Establishing Jewish Life Without a Temple
After the destruction of the Temple, Ribaz gathered the sages of Israel in the vineyard at Yavneh and re-established the Great Beit Din and the Sanhedrin.[1, 2, 3, 14] His central life's work at Yavneh was the enactment of a series of revolutionary halakhic ordinances designed to adapt the Jewish way of life to the new reality without a Temple.[3, 6] These ordinances fell into two main types: enactments that transfer ceremonial powers from the Temple to the "medina" (the rest of the cities of Israel), and enactments that deepen the memory of the Temple in the people's heart out of anticipation of its swift rebuilding.[3, 6]
Below is a detailed, structured summary of the principal enactments of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Moving the Focus of Atonement from the Altar to Acts of Loving-Kindness
The destruction of the Second Temple pulled out from under the nation's feet the traditional mechanism of atonement—the offering of sacrifices on the altar.[13, 16] The theological and existential crisis found tangible expression in a charged encounter between Ribaz and his disciple Rabbi Yehoshua as they left the ruined Jerusalem.[13, 16] At the sight of the burned Temple, Rabbi Yehoshua cried out in tears: "Woe to us that this is destroyed, the place where the sins of Israel were atoned for!"[13, 16]
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's response laid the theological and existential foundation for the life of the nation in exile [13, 16]: "My son, do not be distressed. We have another atonement equal to it—and what is it? Acts of loving-kindness, as it is said: 'For I desire loving-kindness and not sacrifice.'" Ribaz anchored his position in the historical figure of Daniel, the "man of delights," who engaged in acts of loving-kindness, gladdening grooms and accompanying the dead in Babylon, in a period in which it was impossible to offer sacrifices outside the Land of Israel.[16]
This interpretive move was not merely psychological consolation for the moment but a far-reaching theological reform.[9, 16, 17] Ribaz redefined Jewish religiosity and moved the focus of atonement and of the connection with the Divine from the material worship of sacrifices and blood to the moral and social sphere of charity, acts of kindness and mutual support.[9, 16, 17] In this way acts of loving-kindness became the portable altar of the Jewish people in all the places of its dispersion.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Five Disciples: A Typology of Learners, the Mystery of the Chariot, and the Tragedy of Isolation at Emmaus
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai raised five outstanding disciples who became the great Tannaim of the second generation: Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananiah, Rabbi Yose the Priest, Rabbi Shimon ben Netanel, and Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh.[1, 4, 5] Ribaz called each of his disciples by affectionate names and characterized their praise in a way that represents different learning styles and different paths of spiritual development.[1, 4, 5]
In Avot de-Rabbi Natan the extended names of praise that Ribaz gave them appear [5]:
Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus was called "a plastered cistern that does not lose a drop" and also "a pitch-lined jar that preserves its wine," representing the power of preservation and encyclopedic memory that loses nothing of the received tradition.[1, 4, 5]
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananiah was called "a threefold cord that is not quickly broken" (and in the Mishnah: "happy is she who bore him"), pointing to his public resilience and his capacity for leadership in his dealings with emperors and the sages of the nations of the world.[4, 5, 18]
Rabbi Yose the Priest was called "the pious one of the generation" (and in the Mishnah: "pious"), because of his tendency to act beyond the letter of the law.[4, 5, 19]
Rabbi Shimon ben Netanel was called "sin-fearing," expressing extreme caution and dread of the very spiritual blemish even before the stage of punishment.[4, 5, 19]
Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh was called "a flowing stream and an ever-strengthening spring whose waters strengthen and flow outward," representing creative genius, theological innovation and the broadening of the boundaries of halakha from an independent intellectual wellspring.[1, 4, 5]
In tractate Avot the disciples disagreed over the question of what is the good path to which a person should cling in order to merit the World to Come.[5, 19] Rabbi Eliezer proposed "a good eye," Rabbi Yehoshua proposed "a good friend," Rabbi Yose proposed "a good neighbor," Rabbi Shimon proposed "one who foresees the outcome," and Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh proposed "a good heart."[5, 19] Ribaz decided in favor of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh's answer, saying: "I prefer the words of Elazar ben Arakh to your words, for your words are included in his words," since the heart is the main engine and the source from which all the other powers and deeds of a person flow.[5, 19, 20, 21]
The Tragedy of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh and the Need for a Fellowship (Havurah)
Although Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh was classed as the greatest of the disciples—and it was even said of him in the name of Ribaz (by Abba Shaul) that if all the sages of Israel were in one pan of the scale, with Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus among them, and Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh in the other pan, he outweighs them all [1, 5, 22]—this Tanna's end was tragic and instructive.[23, 24]
After Ribaz's death, his colleagues chose to go to Yavneh in order to establish the shared center of Torah.[1, 24] Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh, by contrast, followed his wife to the resort city of Emmaus (Diomsi/Hamat), distinguished for its fine waters and pleasant dwellings, expecting that his colleagues would come to him.[23, 24] His wife persuaded him to stay there, saying: "The bread and the mice—who goes to whom? Surely it is the mice that seek out the bread," that is, the colleagues who need your great Torah will take the trouble and come to you.[24]
Rabbi Elazar remained in Emmaus in complete isolation from his colleagues, and in the absence of mutual enrichment and shared study he gradually forgot all his learning.[23, 24] When his colleagues returned to visit him and asked him simple halakhic questions, he did not know how to answer.[24] His fall reached a terrible breaking point when he stood to read from the Torah the verse "This month shall be for you," and because of his forgetfulness he mistakenly read "Their heart was deaf" (ha-cheresh hayah libam).[23, 24] At the sight of his mistake, those present burst into weeping, and Rabbi Elazar wept with them.[24] His colleagues prayed for mercy on his behalf, and his Torah was restored to him.[23, 24] This tragic story serves in the tradition of the Sages as proof that Torah and wisdom are not the private property of the isolated genius, but are created and preserved solely through connection, dialogue and shared study within a fellowship.[24]
The Account of the Chariot (Maaseh Merkavah) and the Revelation of the Secret
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was one of the foremost masters of esoteric lore of his generation, and the Gemara in tractate Chagigah describes a dramatic mystical encounter between him and Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh on their way.[21] Rabbi Elazar, who was riding behind his teacher on the donkey, asked him: "Master, teach me one chapter of the Account of the Chariot."[21] Ribaz refused at first, in keeping with the rule that one does not expound on the Chariot unless the student is "wise and understands on his own."[21] Rabbi Elazar offered to lecture before Ribaz on something he had learned from him himself.[21]
As soon as Rabbi Elazar began to speak, Ribaz got down from his donkey, wrapped himself in a prayer shawl and sat on a stone beneath an olive tree.[21] When his disciple asked why he had dismounted, Ribaz answered: "It is not proper that I should hear the glory of my Maker while I am riding on a donkey."[21] At that hour fire came down from heaven and surrounded the trees in the field, and the ministering angels accompanied them in excitement.[21] This event testifies to the mystical depth of Ribaz's teaching, which was not confined to existential, earthly halakhot but touched on the secrets of the Supernal Chariot.[6, 22]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Death of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: Existential Anxiety and the Presence of Hezekiah, King of Judah
The last hours of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, as described in tractate Berakhot, reveal the existential anxiety of the leader who carried on his shoulders the burden of the generations of destruction and reconstruction.[8, 10] When Ribaz fell ill and was about to die, his disciples entered to visit him and saw him weeping bitterly.[8, 10]
The astonished disciples addressed him with lofty titles: "Lamp of Israel, right-hand pillar, mighty hammer, why are you weeping?"[8, 10] Ribaz answered them with a piercing comparison between the judgment of flesh and blood and heavenly judgment [10]: were they leading him to judgment before a king of flesh and blood—whose anger, imprisonment and execution are not eternal, and who can be bribed with money or appeased with words—he would be trembling with fear.[10] Now, as he is being led before the King of kings of kings, whose anger and whose execution are eternal and who cannot be appeased with money, and when there are two paths before him—one of the Garden of Eden and one of Gehenna—and he does not know by which path he is being led, how should he not weep?[10]
This weeping, beyond general fear of Heaven, reflected the weight of his historic decision to take the path of "hatzalah portah" and to give up Jerusalem and the Temple.[10] The terrible doubt whether he had erred in his political and spiritual judgment, and whether he should have insisted and demanded the rescue of all of Jerusalem, troubled him deeply until his last moments and left him in complete uncertainty about the rightness of his path in the eyes of the Creator.[10]
Before parting from them, the disciples asked: "Our teacher, bless us."[8, 10] Ribaz blessed them with a profound, practical blessing: "May it be His will that the fear of Heaven be upon you as the fear of flesh and blood."[8, 10] To their astonished question "Only that much?" (is that the highest aspiration?), he answered with existential shrewdness: "Would that it were so! Know that when a person commits a transgression he says, 'May no one see me.'"[8, 10] At the very moment of his death, he instructed them to clear the vessels out of the house to prevent their becoming impure with his death, and he called out: "Prepare a throne for Hezekiah, king of Judah, who is coming."[8, 10]
The Symbolic Meaning of the Arrival of Hezekiah, King of Judah
The spiritual presence of Hezekiah, king of Judah, at the moment of Ribaz's death carries a heavy theological and historical charge.[10] Hezekiah was a king who chose to fight the Assyrian Empire rather than surrender, yet at the same time knew how to make peace, pay taxes and preserve Jerusalem's survival by diplomatic means. The spiritual arrival of Hezekiah, king of Judah, at Ribaz's deathbed constituted a heavenly confirmation and seal of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's path of leadership.[10]
Hezekiah comes to thank Ribaz for having cared not for temporary physical freedom but for the spiritual continuity of the nation, and he confirms the decision to make peace with Rome without a futile war, in order to save Yavneh, the Torah and the dynasty of the House of David.[10] Ribaz's legacy at Yavneh saved the people of Israel from cultural and religious extinction, and proved that Torah is capable of renewing itself and adapting even in the most difficult situations of destruction.[1, 2, 7]

The Work, Teaching and Leadership of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: Reshaping Judaism in an Age of Crisis and Reconstruction
This source surveys the figure of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, the leader who reshaped Judaism after the destruction of the Second Temple. The text details how Ribaz acted with political shrewdness toward the Roman Empire in order to save the world of Torah, and how he established the spiritual center at Yavneh as a substitute for political sovereignty in Jerusalem. Through a series of halakhic enactments and theological reforms, he moved the focus of atonement and holiness from the sacrificial service to acts of loving-kindness and the study of Torah, thereby securing the nation's survival in exile. Beyond his public work, the source discusses him as a humble educator who stressed the importance of a good heart and of shared study, presenting his relations with his five outstanding disciples and his formative influence on later generations.
The Work, Teaching and Leadership of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: Reshaping Judaism in an Age of Crisis and Reconstruction
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's Standing in the Schools of Hillel and Shammai, and His Conception of Torah Study
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai (called Zakkai or Zakkayi in the literature of the Land of Israel, and "Ribaz" for short) was active in the first century CE and became the key figure in the dramatic transition of the Jewish people from the destruction of the Second Temple to an era of reconstruction and halakhic creativity.[1, 2, 3] Ribaz acquired his Torah from Hillel the Elder and Shammai the Elder.[1, 2, 3, 4] In the school of Hillel's disciples, which numbered eighty outstanding students, Ribaz was classed as "the least of them all," while Jonathan ben Uzziel was classed as "the greatest of them all."[5] This classification of Hillel's disciples placed thirty of them as worthy of having the Divine Presence rest upon them as it did upon Moses our teacher, thirty as worthy of intercalating the year, and twenty as middling.[5]
Despite his classification as "least" in the school—a designation that points to his being the youngest of the disciples or the last of them—Ribaz displayed complete mastery of every recess of the Oral Torah.[5] It was said of him that he left unstudied no Scripture, Mishnah, Gemara, halakhot, aggadot, Tosefta, fine points of the Torah or fine points of the scribes, light matters and weighty ones, verbal analogies (gezerot shavot), calendrical cycles, gematriot, and even esoteric fields such as the speech of the ministering angels, the speech of demons, the speech of palm trees, and the parables of launderers and foxes.[3, 5, 6] This recognition of his abilities led Hillel the Elder to grant him the formative title "father of wisdom and father of the generations," defining him as a head of the sages and a guide for all the generations to come.[3, 6, 7]
Ribaz's educational teaching completely rejected intellectual and scholarly arrogance.[7] Although he had acquired phenomenal knowledge, he used to warn his many disciples against conceit, saying: "If you have learned much Torah, do not take credit for yourself—for it was for this that you were created."[4, 5, 8] This remark reflects a profound cosmic conception, according to which Torah is not an act of personal heroism that confers privilege or honor, but a fundamental existential duty.[4, 5] Human existence is conditional upon accepting the Torah and laboring in it, as emerges from the tradition that the Holy One, blessed be He, stipulated with the work of Creation that if Israel does not accept the Torah, the world will revert to chaos and void; study is therefore the fulfillment of a condition of Creation and not a voluntary act of piety.[4]
Ribaz's way of life exemplified a complete synthesis between rigorous scholarship and humility and social piety.[7] He took care to be the first to arrive at the study hall, did not waste a moment of his learning, and never engaged in idle talk or walked four cubits without Torah and tefillin.[3, 6, 7] His moral path stressed love of fellow creatures and being first to greet every person in the marketplace, even gentiles.[6, 7]
In the economic and social sphere, Ribaz developed a distinctive doctrine concerning the commandment of charity.[7] He demanded that those around him give charity abundantly and used to say that he gives nothing of his own but only from the Creator's property, so there is no reason to be tight-fisted.[7] In his view, although a person's sustenance is apportioned to him from one Rosh Hashanah to the next, God deducts the charity money a person has given from the list of losses and afflictions decreed against him, so that charity becomes an economic and spiritual shield.[7]
This conception of the protection afforded by Torah and charity found expression when a Jerusalem family came to him, all of whose sons had died before the age of eighteen.[7, 9] Ribaz identified them as descendants of Eli the priest, upon whom early death had been decreed because of the sins of Hophni and Phinehas, and proposed that they engage in Torah and acts of loving-kindness as a spiritual protective mechanism that would free them from the curse.[7, 9] The members of the family accepted his advice, engaged in Torah and kindness, and lived long lives.[7, 9]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Political Policy and the Edicts Against Zealotry on the Eve of the Destruction
During the Great Revolt and the Roman siege of Jerusalem, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai stood out as a moderate, peace-seeking leader who preferred political compromise to hopeless military zealotry.[3] Like his teacher Hillel, Ribaz recoiled from acts of religious zealotry that take no account of political reality.[3] His pragmatic position was formulated in his well-known warning against demolishing the high places and foreign cults of the gentiles in the Land of Israel: "Do not rush to tear down the gentiles' high places lest you be made to build them with your own hands—lest you tear down ones of brick and they tell you, 'Make them of stone'; of stone, and they tell you, 'Make them of wood.'"[3] This warning reflects a strategic view that understands that zealous acts of provocation against foreign authorities do not help to purify the land but invite a harsh counter-reaction and worsen the burden of subjugation and the destruction of the Jewish settlement.[3]
When the siege of Jerusalem began, Ribaz sat inside the city and watched with alarm the conduct of the zealot factions, called in the sources "the biryonim" (the thugs).[3] The zealots burned the city's stores of grain and food in order to force the inhabitants to fight the Romans out of despair.[3] Ribaz, who saw people boiling straw in order to drink its water because of deep hunger, understood that the city could not withstand the siege of the commander Vespasian and that continued fighting would lead to mass slaughter and the extinction of Torah.[3] He concluded that the zealots' plans must be foiled and that he must flee the city in order to save the core of the spiritual leadership.[1, 3]
The plan to smuggle him out of Jerusalem was based on deceiving the zealot guards at the city gates.[1, 3] Ribaz turned in secret to the head of the biryonim, Abba Sikra (ben Batiah), who was his nephew, and enlisted his help.[3] Following his instruction, Ribaz feigned serious illness and then death.[3] His two outstanding disciples, Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananiah, placed him in a coffin and carried him to the city gates, knowing that the zealots permitted the dead to be taken out for burial outside the walls because of the sanctity of Jerusalem.[3, 10]
At the city gates the operation faced a real danger of failure.[3] The zealot guards suspected the coffin and wished to stab it with a sword or push it to make sure of death.[3] Abba Sikra prevented them with tactical arguments, warning that such acts would disgrace the leader's honor in the eyes of the public ("They will say: they stabbed the Rabban, they pushed the Rabban").[3] The guards withdrew, and Ribaz was successfully smuggled outside the walls directly to the Roman camp.[3, 10]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Meeting with Vespasian: The Paradox of the Honey Barrel and the Dragon, and the Strategy of "Hatzalah Portah"
Upon reaching the Roman camp, Ribaz met the commander Vespasian and addressed him with the royal greeting "Peace upon you, O king."[3, 10] Vespasian reacted in anger and claimed that Ribaz was a rebel liable to death twice: first, because he called him king though he was not king; and second, because if he really was king, why had Ribaz not come to him until now.[3, 8, 10, 11] Ribaz answered his questions with political and exegetical shrewdness.[12] To the first question he replied that Vespasian was soon to be appointed emperor, since the Temple and Jerusalem are destined to fall only into the hands of a king, as it is said, "And Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one," and "mighty" means nothing other than a king.[12] To the second question he replied that the biryonim who ruled Jerusalem had prevented him from leaving and coming to him.[12]
While they were conversing, an official Roman messenger arrived and informed Vespasian that the emperor had died and that the notables of Rome had appointed him the new emperor.[3, 10, 12] The event brought a dramatic turn in the emperor's attitude toward Ribaz.[3, 10] Vespasian valued the Tanna's wisdom and offered him to ask one request that he would fulfill for him.[3, 10]
In the course of this discussion, Vespasian presented Ribaz with a pointed parable challenging his moderate path [12]: "If people had a barrel of honey with a dragon (serpent) coiled around it, would they not break the barrel in order to kill the dragon?" In this parable the barrel represents Jerusalem and the Temple, and the dragon represents the rebel zealots. Vespasian argued that there was no escaping the destruction of the entire city in order to eradicate the rebels within it.[12] Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was silent and did not answer this parable.[12]
Ribaz's silence drew pointed criticism from later sages.[8, 10, 11] The Gemara notes that Rav Yosef (some say Rabbi Akiva) applied to him the verse "He turns wise men backward, and makes their knowledge foolish," claiming that he should have answered Vespasian: "We take tongs, we remove the dragon and kill it, and we leave the barrel alone" (that is, one takes tongs, removes the serpent and kills it, and leaves the barrel whole).[12] According to this criticism, Ribaz missed a historic opportunity to demand the rescue of Jerusalem and the Temple from the Romans.[8, 10, 11]
But Ribaz's silence and his limited requests stemmed from a calculated strategy of political realism.[8, 10, 11] Ribaz assessed that too large a demand for the rescue of all of Jerusalem would be rejected out of hand by an emperor determined to display a crushing military victory, and as a result everything would be lost.[8, 10, 11] He chose to prefer the strategy of "hatzalah portah" (a small but certain rescue) in order to secure the nation's future, and made three focused requests [8, 10, 11]:
"Give me Yavneh and its sages": saving the sages of the generation and establishing a Torah and legal center as an alternative to Jerusalem.[3, 10, 13]
"The dynasty (shushilta) of Rabban Gamliel": ensuring the safety of the members of the patriarchal family of the House of Hillel, in order to preserve legitimate and recognized national leadership and to prevent anarchy.[3, 10]
"And physicians to heal Rabbi Zadok": doctors who would heal Rabbi Zadok, who was a symbol of the righteous man who had fasted forty consecutive years to prevent the destruction and whose body was in extreme mortal danger.[3, 10]
Through these three requests, Ribaz laid the foundation for the continued existence of the people of Israel as a living, developing spiritual community without need of a sovereign political and Temple center.[1, 3, 13]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Enactments at Yavneh as the Foundation for Establishing Jewish Life Without a Temple
After the destruction of the Temple, Ribaz gathered the sages of Israel in the vineyard at Yavneh and re-established the Great Beit Din and the Sanhedrin.[1, 2, 3, 14] His central life's work at Yavneh was the enactment of a series of revolutionary halakhic ordinances designed to adapt the Jewish way of life to the new reality without a Temple.[3, 6] These ordinances fell into two main types: enactments that transfer ceremonial powers from the Temple to the "medina" (the rest of the cities of Israel), and enactments that deepen the memory of the Temple in the people's heart out of anticipation of its swift rebuilding.[3, 6]
Below is a detailed, structured summary of the principal enactments of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Moving the Focus of Atonement from the Altar to Acts of Loving-Kindness
The destruction of the Second Temple pulled out from under the nation's feet the traditional mechanism of atonement—the offering of sacrifices on the altar.[13, 16] The theological and existential crisis found tangible expression in a charged encounter between Ribaz and his disciple Rabbi Yehoshua as they left the ruined Jerusalem.[13, 16] At the sight of the burned Temple, Rabbi Yehoshua cried out in tears: "Woe to us that this is destroyed, the place where the sins of Israel were atoned for!"[13, 16]
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's response laid the theological and existential foundation for the life of the nation in exile [13, 16]: "My son, do not be distressed. We have another atonement equal to it—and what is it? Acts of loving-kindness, as it is said: 'For I desire loving-kindness and not sacrifice.'" Ribaz anchored his position in the historical figure of Daniel, the "man of delights," who engaged in acts of loving-kindness, gladdening grooms and accompanying the dead in Babylon, in a period in which it was impossible to offer sacrifices outside the Land of Israel.[16]
This interpretive move was not merely psychological consolation for the moment but a far-reaching theological reform.[9, 16, 17] Ribaz redefined Jewish religiosity and moved the focus of atonement and of the connection with the Divine from the material worship of sacrifices and blood to the moral and social sphere of charity, acts of kindness and mutual support.[9, 16, 17] In this way acts of loving-kindness became the portable altar of the Jewish people in all the places of its dispersion.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Five Disciples: A Typology of Learners, the Mystery of the Chariot, and the Tragedy of Isolation at Emmaus
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai raised five outstanding disciples who became the great Tannaim of the second generation: Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananiah, Rabbi Yose the Priest, Rabbi Shimon ben Netanel, and Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh.[1, 4, 5] Ribaz called each of his disciples by affectionate names and characterized their praise in a way that represents different learning styles and different paths of spiritual development.[1, 4, 5]
In Avot de-Rabbi Natan the extended names of praise that Ribaz gave them appear [5]:
Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus was called "a plastered cistern that does not lose a drop" and also "a pitch-lined jar that preserves its wine," representing the power of preservation and encyclopedic memory that loses nothing of the received tradition.[1, 4, 5]
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananiah was called "a threefold cord that is not quickly broken" (and in the Mishnah: "happy is she who bore him"), pointing to his public resilience and his capacity for leadership in his dealings with emperors and the sages of the nations of the world.[4, 5, 18]
Rabbi Yose the Priest was called "the pious one of the generation" (and in the Mishnah: "pious"), because of his tendency to act beyond the letter of the law.[4, 5, 19]
Rabbi Shimon ben Netanel was called "sin-fearing," expressing extreme caution and dread of the very spiritual blemish even before the stage of punishment.[4, 5, 19]
Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh was called "a flowing stream and an ever-strengthening spring whose waters strengthen and flow outward," representing creative genius, theological innovation and the broadening of the boundaries of halakha from an independent intellectual wellspring.[1, 4, 5]
In tractate Avot the disciples disagreed over the question of what is the good path to which a person should cling in order to merit the World to Come.[5, 19] Rabbi Eliezer proposed "a good eye," Rabbi Yehoshua proposed "a good friend," Rabbi Yose proposed "a good neighbor," Rabbi Shimon proposed "one who foresees the outcome," and Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh proposed "a good heart."[5, 19] Ribaz decided in favor of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh's answer, saying: "I prefer the words of Elazar ben Arakh to your words, for your words are included in his words," since the heart is the main engine and the source from which all the other powers and deeds of a person flow.[5, 19, 20, 21]
The Tragedy of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh and the Need for a Fellowship (Havurah)
Although Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh was classed as the greatest of the disciples—and it was even said of him in the name of Ribaz (by Abba Shaul) that if all the sages of Israel were in one pan of the scale, with Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus among them, and Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh in the other pan, he outweighs them all [1, 5, 22]—this Tanna's end was tragic and instructive.[23, 24]
After Ribaz's death, his colleagues chose to go to Yavneh in order to establish the shared center of Torah.[1, 24] Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh, by contrast, followed his wife to the resort city of Emmaus (Diomsi/Hamat), distinguished for its fine waters and pleasant dwellings, expecting that his colleagues would come to him.[23, 24] His wife persuaded him to stay there, saying: "The bread and the mice—who goes to whom? Surely it is the mice that seek out the bread," that is, the colleagues who need your great Torah will take the trouble and come to you.[24]
Rabbi Elazar remained in Emmaus in complete isolation from his colleagues, and in the absence of mutual enrichment and shared study he gradually forgot all his learning.[23, 24] When his colleagues returned to visit him and asked him simple halakhic questions, he did not know how to answer.[24] His fall reached a terrible breaking point when he stood to read from the Torah the verse "This month shall be for you," and because of his forgetfulness he mistakenly read "Their heart was deaf" (ha-cheresh hayah libam).[23, 24] At the sight of his mistake, those present burst into weeping, and Rabbi Elazar wept with them.[24] His colleagues prayed for mercy on his behalf, and his Torah was restored to him.[23, 24] This tragic story serves in the tradition of the Sages as proof that Torah and wisdom are not the private property of the isolated genius, but are created and preserved solely through connection, dialogue and shared study within a fellowship.[24]
The Account of the Chariot (Maaseh Merkavah) and the Revelation of the Secret
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was one of the foremost masters of esoteric lore of his generation, and the Gemara in tractate Chagigah describes a dramatic mystical encounter between him and Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh on their way.[21] Rabbi Elazar, who was riding behind his teacher on the donkey, asked him: "Master, teach me one chapter of the Account of the Chariot."[21] Ribaz refused at first, in keeping with the rule that one does not expound on the Chariot unless the student is "wise and understands on his own."[21] Rabbi Elazar offered to lecture before Ribaz on something he had learned from him himself.[21]
As soon as Rabbi Elazar began to speak, Ribaz got down from his donkey, wrapped himself in a prayer shawl and sat on a stone beneath an olive tree.[21] When his disciple asked why he had dismounted, Ribaz answered: "It is not proper that I should hear the glory of my Maker while I am riding on a donkey."[21] At that hour fire came down from heaven and surrounded the trees in the field, and the ministering angels accompanied them in excitement.[21] This event testifies to the mystical depth of Ribaz's teaching, which was not confined to existential, earthly halakhot but touched on the secrets of the Supernal Chariot.[6, 22]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Death of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: Existential Anxiety and the Presence of Hezekiah, King of Judah
The last hours of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, as described in tractate Berakhot, reveal the existential anxiety of the leader who carried on his shoulders the burden of the generations of destruction and reconstruction.[8, 10] When Ribaz fell ill and was about to die, his disciples entered to visit him and saw him weeping bitterly.[8, 10]
The astonished disciples addressed him with lofty titles: "Lamp of Israel, right-hand pillar, mighty hammer, why are you weeping?"[8, 10] Ribaz answered them with a piercing comparison between the judgment of flesh and blood and heavenly judgment [10]: were they leading him to judgment before a king of flesh and blood—whose anger, imprisonment and execution are not eternal, and who can be bribed with money or appeased with words—he would be trembling with fear.[10] Now, as he is being led before the King of kings of kings, whose anger and whose execution are eternal and who cannot be appeased with money, and when there are two paths before him—one of the Garden of Eden and one of Gehenna—and he does not know by which path he is being led, how should he not weep?[10]
This weeping, beyond general fear of Heaven, reflected the weight of his historic decision to take the path of "hatzalah portah" and to give up Jerusalem and the Temple.[10] The terrible doubt whether he had erred in his political and spiritual judgment, and whether he should have insisted and demanded the rescue of all of Jerusalem, troubled him deeply until his last moments and left him in complete uncertainty about the rightness of his path in the eyes of the Creator.[10]
Before parting from them, the disciples asked: "Our teacher, bless us."[8, 10] Ribaz blessed them with a profound, practical blessing: "May it be His will that the fear of Heaven be upon you as the fear of flesh and blood."[8, 10] To their astonished question "Only that much?" (is that the highest aspiration?), he answered with existential shrewdness: "Would that it were so! Know that when a person commits a transgression he says, 'May no one see me.'"[8, 10] At the very moment of his death, he instructed them to clear the vessels out of the house to prevent their becoming impure with his death, and he called out: "Prepare a throne for Hezekiah, king of Judah, who is coming."[8, 10]
The Symbolic Meaning of the Arrival of Hezekiah, King of Judah
The spiritual presence of Hezekiah, king of Judah, at the moment of Ribaz's death carries a heavy theological and historical charge.[10] Hezekiah was a king who chose to fight the Assyrian Empire rather than surrender, yet at the same time knew how to make peace, pay taxes and preserve Jerusalem's survival by diplomatic means. The spiritual arrival of Hezekiah, king of Judah, at Ribaz's deathbed constituted a heavenly confirmation and seal of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's path of leadership.[10]
Hezekiah comes to thank Ribaz for having cared not for temporary physical freedom but for the spiritual continuity of the nation, and he confirms the decision to make peace with Rome without a futile war, in order to save Yavneh, the Torah and the dynasty of the House of David.[10] Ribaz's legacy at Yavneh saved the people of Israel from cultural and religious extinction, and proved that Torah is capable of renewing itself and adapting even in the most difficult situations of destruction.[1, 2, 7]
